summaryEn: Ten straight quarters of losses ended in one quarter, and the next one tripled it: gross margin went from 13% to 64% as Samsung and Kioxia walked away from a memory market Macronix could still serve. Pricing power created by other people's exits is real — and it is the kind that comes back.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + company announcements; memory-cycle framing — the end of ten loss quarters, the three verified drivers (NOR pricing on HBM4, MLC NAND order transfer after Samsung's exit and Kioxia's EOL notices, Switch 2 ROM) and the 2026Q2 results credited with the newer-than-feed data explicitly flagged, but the trailing P/E of 0.00 stripped and the trailing −1.29% ROE explained as obsolete, and the central caution stated: pricing power created by competitors' exit is reversible, and NT$15.8bn of capex into a shortage is the memory industry's classic error; sector Semiconductors → NOR Flash & Memory)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Macronix (旺宏電子, TWSE: 2337) makes **NOR Flash, ROM and NAND memory** — the chips that store the code a device runs at startup, the read-only cartridges of games consoles, and the embedded storage inside industrial and consumer products. Founded in **1989** and **listed in March 1995**, it spent the last three years in one of the worst downturns of its history, and has just come out of it with unusual violence.

**The company recorded ten consecutive loss-making quarters.** Annual EPS ran **NT$4.85 (FY2022) → −0.92 (FY2023) → −1.72 (FY2024) → −NT$1.78 (FY2025)**. Gross margin fell to **13.2%** and operating margin to **−29.6%**. The dividend stopped after FY2023.

Then, in **2026Q1: revenue of NT$10.469bn (+71% year-on-year), gross margin of 40.8%, and EPS of NT$0.90** — the first profit in ten quarters. **And 2026Q2, announced on 28 July 2026, was substantially larger again: revenue of NT$19.125bn (+83% sequentially, +181% year-on-year), gross margin of 64.4%, and EPS of NT$3.91**, against a loss of NT$0.69 a year earlier. The company also announced a **capital expenditure programme of NT$15.8bn**. *(The metric tables on this page run through 2026Q1, which is what the data feed carries; the Q2 figures come from the company's announcement.)*

**Three drivers explain it, and all three are verified.** First, **NOR Flash pricing**: as AI servers move to HBM4, NOR content rises by roughly **50%**, and Macronix used monthly repricing to push first-quarter quotes up about **30%**. Second, and larger, **MLC NAND**: **Samsung discontinued MLC production and Kioxia issued end-of-life notices**, leaving very few suppliers able to offer **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB** — a market the majors handed over. **Macronix's NAND revenue rose 90% sequentially and 382% year-on-year in Q1**, with **32GB eMMC entering mass production in the second quarter**. Third, the **Nintendo Switch 2 ROM business**, which provides steady support rather than explosive growth.

Two reported figures on this page need explaining. **Return on equity shows −1.29%** because it is a trailing twelve-month measure still containing three loss quarters — it is already obsolete. And the **reported price-to-earnings ratio of 0.00× has been removed**, being meaningless on a loss-making trailing period. What the data does show cleanly is the turn: gross margin **13.2% → 24.2% → 40.8%**, operating margin **−29.6% → +18.5%**, and monthly revenue running **+51%, +60%, +96%, +154%, +176%, +216%**.

The caution is straightforward and important. **This pricing power exists because competitors left.** That is genuinely valuable while it lasts, and it is precisely the kind of advantage that reverses when capacity returns — and **NT$15.8bn of capital expenditure committed into a shortage is the memory industry's most reliably repeated mistake.** The honest read: **a spectacular, well-evidenced recovery built on other companies' withdrawal, in the most cyclical business in semiconductors.**

Macronix was founded in **1989**, among the first wave of Taiwanese integrated device manufacturers — companies that both design and fabricate their own chips, rather than splitting the two as the foundry model later encouraged. It **listed in 1995**, and specialised in **non-volatile memory**: chips that retain data when power is removed.

Its particular niche was **NOR Flash and ROM**, which are less glamorous than the DRAM and NAND that dominate memory headlines but are quietly essential. **NOR Flash** allows a processor to execute code directly from it, which makes it the natural place to store the firmware a device runs at startup — in cars, industrial controllers, networking equipment and servers. **Mask ROM** is written once at manufacture and never changed, which made Macronix the supplier of choice for **games console cartridges**, a business it has held across multiple Nintendo generations.

These are demanding, long-lifecycle markets. An automotive or industrial customer needs the same part available for a decade, qualified and unchanged. That favours a supplier willing to maintain mature process nodes — which the largest memory manufacturers, whose economics depend on migrating to the newest node at the largest scale, increasingly are not.

**That asymmetry is what produced the current situation.** As **Samsung discontinued MLC NAND production and Kioxia issued end-of-life notices** on their older-generation parts, they vacated a market that customers still needed served. Very few suppliers can offer **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB** — and Macronix could. Simultaneously, **AI servers moving to HBM4 raised NOR Flash content by around 50%**, tightening a market Macronix already served.

The result, after **ten consecutive quarters of losses**, was a reversal of extraordinary speed: **gross margin from 13.2% to 64.4% in five quarters**, and quarterly EPS from **−NT$0.15 to +NT$3.91**. It is a reminder of what the memory industry does — and that the survivor of a brutal downturn inherits the pricing power of everyone who left.

- **1989 (9 Dec)** — Macronix founded as an integrated device manufacturer specialising in **non-volatile memory**.
- **1995 (15 March)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2337)**.
- **1990s–2010s** — Builds leading positions in **NOR Flash** and **mask ROM**, including games console cartridge supply across multiple Nintendo generations, plus NAND and automotive and industrial memory.
- **2022** — A strong year: **FY2022 EPS NT$4.85**; dividend **NT$1.8**.
- **2023** — The downturn begins: **FY2023 EPS −NT$0.92**; dividend cut to **NT$0.5** — the last paid.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS −NT$1.72**; Q4 gross margin falls to **13.2%** and operating margin to **−29.6%**.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS −NT$1.78**, completing **ten consecutive loss-making quarters**. Gross margin begins recovering, reaching **24.2%** in Q4.
- **Industry shift** — **Samsung discontinues MLC NAND production; Kioxia issues end-of-life notices**, leaving few suppliers able to serve **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB**. Separately, **AI servers moving to HBM4 raise NOR Flash content by about 50%**.
- **2026Q1** — **The turn: revenue NT$10.469bn (+71% YoY), gross margin 40.8%, operating margin 18.5%, EPS NT$0.90** — the first profit in ten quarters. **NAND revenue up 90% sequentially and 382% year-on-year**; monthly repricing lifts NOR quotes about **30%**.
- **2026Q2 (announced 28 July 2026)** — **Revenue NT$19.125bn (+83% QoQ, +181% YoY), gross margin 64.4%, EPS NT$3.91** against a **NT$0.69 loss** a year earlier. **32GB eMMC enters mass production.** A **NT$15.8bn capital expenditure programme** is announced.
- **2026 (to June)** — Monthly revenue growth runs **+51%, +60%, +96%, +154%, +176%, +216%**.

Macronix's accounts show **the sharpest reversal in this collection, and two trailing figures that have not caught up with it**.

- **Three years of losses.** Annual EPS: **NT$4.85 (FY2022) → −0.92 (FY2023) → −1.72 (FY2024) → −NT$1.78 (FY2025)** — **ten consecutive loss-making quarters**, with gross margin bottoming at **13.2%** and operating margin at **−29.6%** in 2024Q4.
- **The recovery, quarter by quarter.** Gross margin: **13.2% (2024Q4) → 17.7% → 15.7% → 13.5% → 24.2% (2025Q4) → 40.8% (2026Q1) → 64.4% (2026Q2)**. Operating margin: **−29.6% → +18.5%** by 2026Q1. EPS: **−NT$0.15 (2025Q4) → +NT$0.90 (2026Q1) → +NT$3.91 (2026Q2)**.
- **The Q2 figures are newer than the metric tables.** **2026Q2 revenue of NT$19.125bn (+83% sequentially, +181% year-on-year), gross margin 64.4% and EPS NT$3.91** come from the company's announcement of **28 July 2026**. The tables on this page run through **2026Q1**, which is what the data feed carries — the difference is stated here rather than left for the reader to discover.
- **Two trailing figures are already obsolete, and one has been removed.** **Return on equity of −1.29%** is a trailing twelve-month measure still containing three loss quarters. And the **reported price-to-earnings ratio of 0.00× has been stripped from this page** as meaningless on a loss-making trailing basis — the shares trade at **NT$113.00 and 4.42× book**.
- **Revenue growth is accelerating, not merely positive.** Monthly year-on-year growth: **+51%, +60%, +96%, +154%, +176%, +216%**.
- **The balance sheet supported the downturn.** **NT$82.15bn of assets** on **NT$50.65bn of equity** — a **38.4% debt ratio** — with **NT$15.97bn of cash**. **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$2.19bn exceeded NT$1.78bn of net income**, so the recovery is generating cash.
- **No dividend since FY2023.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.2 (2018) → 1.19 → 1.2 → 1.8 (2021) → 1.8 (2022) → NT$0.5 (2023)**, and nothing since. **Dividend yield is 0.00%**, accurately.
- **Capital spending of NT$15.8bn** has been committed to expand capacity.

The financing reality: **a company that survived a three-year memory downturn with an intact balance sheet and is now earning at a rate the trailing statistics have not yet registered — while committing substantial capital into the conditions that produced it.**

**Stance: a memory maker that ended ten loss quarters and then tripled its earnings in the next one, because Samsung and Kioxia left a market it could still serve — pricing power that is real, and reversible.**

The bull case:

1. **The turn is documented, not projected.** **2026Q1: revenue +71%, gross margin 40.8%, EPS NT$0.90.** **2026Q2: revenue NT$19.125bn (+181% year-on-year), gross margin 64.4%, EPS NT$3.91.** Monthly revenue growth reached **+216%**.
2. **The cause is structural, not merely cyclical.** **Samsung discontinued MLC NAND and Kioxia issued end-of-life notices**, and very few suppliers can serve **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB**. Macronix stepped directly into demand the majors abandoned — **NAND revenue up 90% sequentially and 382% year-on-year** — with **32GB eMMC into mass production** in Q2.
3. **A second, AI-linked driver.** **AI servers moving to HBM4 raise NOR Flash content by about 50%**, and monthly repricing lifted Q1 NOR quotes roughly **30%**.
4. **A third, stabilising one.** **Nintendo Switch 2 ROM** provides steady baseline demand rather than a spike.
5. **The balance sheet came through intact.** **38.4% debt ratio**, **NT$15.97bn cash**, and **operating cash flow above net income** in the first recovery quarter.

The counter-arguments:

- **The advantage was created by others' exit, and exits reverse.** Pricing power that comes from competitors leaving is genuine and temporary. If demand justifies it, capacity returns — from the same majors or from others.
- **NT$15.8bn of capex into a shortage is the memory industry's signature mistake.** Capacity ordered at the top has repeatedly delivered into the bottom.
- **Memory is the most cyclical business in semiconductors.** This company earned **NT$4.85 in FY2022 and lost money for the following ten quarters**. Neither extreme is the normal state.
- **The trailing statistics mislead in both directions** — a **−1.29% ROE** and a stripped **0.00× P/E** now, and shortly a very low P/E on peak earnings, which is the classic trap in cyclicals.
- **No dividend since FY2023.**

A **cycle-inflection** thesis: an exceptionally strong, verifiable recovery — bought with full awareness that memory pricing power is borrowed from whoever is not currently competing.

Macronix designs **and manufactures** its own memory chips — an integrated device manufacturer, not a fabless designer — across three product families with different economics:

- **NOR Flash.** Memory a processor can **execute code directly from**, which makes it the standard place to store firmware and boot code in cars, industrial controllers, networking equipment and servers. Volumes are modest and lifecycles are long — customers need the same qualified part for years. **AI servers moving to HBM4 raise NOR content by about 50%**, and because supply is concentrated, Macronix was able to reprice **monthly**, lifting Q1 quotes around **30%**.
- **Mask ROM.** Written once during manufacture and unchangeable — the technology behind **games console cartridges**, where Macronix has supplied across multiple Nintendo generations, currently including **Switch 2**. Predictable, tied to console cycles.
- **NAND, including MLC and eMMC.** Higher-density storage. This is where the largest change occurred: **Samsung discontinued MLC production and Kioxia issued end-of-life notices**, and few suppliers can offer **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB**. Macronix took that demand — **NAND revenue up 90% sequentially and 382% year-on-year** in Q1 — and brought **32GB eMMC to mass production** in Q2.
- **Why being willing to run mature nodes is the whole strategy.** The largest memory manufacturers earn their returns by **migrating to the newest node at the greatest scale**; maintaining older processes for smaller, long-lifecycle customers is a poor use of their capital. Macronix's business is precisely those customers — which is why, when the majors exited, the demand did not disappear, it moved.
- **The cost structure, and why margins swing so far.** Owning fabs means **enormous fixed costs**. At low utilisation and weak pricing, gross margin collapsed to **13.2%**; at high utilisation and firm pricing, it reached **64.4%**. Nothing about the products changed between those two points.

The levers are **memory pricing, utilisation, product mix and competitor capacity decisions**. The strength is a defensible niche the majors have chosen to leave, in products with long qualification and long lifecycles. The vulnerability is inherent: **a fab-owning memory company has extreme operating leverage in both directions**, and its current advantage depends on others continuing to stay away.

Memory is the most cyclical business in semiconductors, and this cycle turned for an unusual reason.

- **The normal mechanism.** Memory is a commodity produced in enormous fabs that must run continuously. When demand softens, everyone keeps producing, prices collapse, and the whole industry loses money — as **Nanya Technology (2408)** elsewhere in this collection shows in DRAM. When demand recovers against fixed capacity, prices rise faster than anyone expects. Macronix's **ten consecutive loss quarters followed by a 64.4% gross margin** is that mechanism at full amplitude.
- **What made this turn different.** It was not only demand recovering — **supply was actively withdrawn**. **Samsung discontinued MLC NAND production and Kioxia issued end-of-life notices** on older-generation parts. For the majors this is rational: capital belongs on the newest, densest nodes. But the customers using those parts — industrial, automotive, embedded — cannot simply migrate, because their products are qualified around specific memory. **The demand stayed and the supply left.**
- **Who could serve it.** Very few. Offering **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB** requires maintaining mature process capability that most manufacturers have retired. Macronix had it, which is why its **NAND revenue rose 382% year-on-year**.
- **The NOR side.** NOR Flash is a concentrated market — Macronix, **Winbond (2344)** and a handful of others. **AI servers upgrading to HBM4 raise NOR content by about 50%**, tightening supply in a market that had already consolidated.
- **The console business.** Mask ROM for games cartridges is a niche with few credible suppliers and multi-year platform cycles, currently supported by **Switch 2**.
- **What happens next, historically.** High margins attract capacity. Macronix has committed **NT$15.8bn of capital expenditure**; if the economics persist, others will follow, including the majors who left. **Shortage-driven pricing in memory has never been permanent**, and the industry's history is of capacity arriving precisely as demand normalises.

Macronix's position is **genuinely advantaged right now**, in niches the largest players have deliberately vacated. The industry truth is that **memory rewards the survivor of a downturn with the pricing power of everyone who left — and then invites them back.**

**Strengths**
- **Ten consecutive loss quarters ended**: gross margin **13.2% → 40.8% (2026Q1) → 64.4% (2026Q2)**; EPS **−NT$0.15 → +NT$0.90 → +NT$3.91**.
- **Structural gap created by others' exit**: Samsung discontinued MLC, Kioxia issued EOL; few suppliers offer **19nm 2D and 3D MLC across 4–32GB**. **NAND revenue +382% YoY**.
- **AI-linked NOR demand**: HBM4 raising NOR content ~**50%**; monthly repricing lifted Q1 quotes ~**30%**.
- **Balance sheet intact**: **38.4% debt ratio**, **NT$15.97bn cash**, operating cash flow above net income.
- **Nintendo Switch 2 ROM** providing steady baseline demand.

**Weaknesses**
- **Three years of losses** immediately behind it; **trailing ROE −1.29%**; reported P/E of 0.00× removed as meaningless.
- **No dividend since FY2023**.
- Fab ownership creates extreme operating leverage in both directions.

**Opportunities**
- **32GB eMMC in mass production** from 2Q26; further MLC share as majors stay out.
- Continued AI server NOR content growth; automotive and industrial long-lifecycle demand.

**Threats**
- **Competitors returning** to the markets they vacated, removing the pricing power.
- **NT$15.8bn of capex** delivering into a normalised market — the memory industry's classic error.
- Demand normalisation after restocking; the low P/E on peak earnings trap.

- **The pricing power was created by other companies leaving (the defining risk).** **Samsung discontinued MLC and Kioxia issued end-of-life notices**, and Macronix stepped into the gap. That is a genuine and valuable position — and it is contingent on those companies, or others, continuing to stay out. Memory margins of **64.4%** are a powerful invitation to return.
- **NT$15.8bn of capital expenditure into a shortage.** This is the memory industry's most reliably repeated mistake: capacity ordered at peak pricing delivers two to three years later, frequently into a market that has normalised. The commitment is rational given current demand and dangerous given history.
- **Extreme cyclicality, demonstrated by this company's own record.** **FY2022 EPS of NT$4.85**, then **ten consecutive loss-making quarters**, then **NT$3.91 in a single quarter**. Neither the trough nor the peak describes a normal year, and averaging across a full cycle is the only sound basis for valuation.
- **The trailing statistics mislead in both directions.** The reported **ROE of −1.29%** and the removed **P/E of 0.00×** understate the company today. Within a few quarters, trailing earnings will make the P/E look very low — which in a cyclical business at peak margins is the classic trap, not a bargain signal.
- **Demand may include restocking.** Part of the **+216% monthly revenue growth** may reflect customers rebuilding inventory after end-of-life notices, which is a one-time effect rather than a run rate.
- **No dividend since FY2023**, so there is no income while the cycle plays out.

Macronix's outlook depends on **how long the supply gap stays open, and what arrives when it closes.** The axes to watch:

- **Gross margin.** The cleanest signal in the business, and currently extraordinary: **13.2% (2024Q4) → 40.8% (2026Q1) → 64.4% (2026Q2)**. A 64% gross margin in memory reflects scarcity pricing; the rate at which it normalises will define the earnings trajectory more than volume will.
- **Competitor behaviour.** The single most important external variable. Any indication that **Samsung, Kioxia or others are re-entering MLC NAND** or expanding NOR capacity would signal the end of the current pricing environment well before it shows up in results.
- **The NT$15.8bn capital expenditure programme.** When the capacity arrives and what pricing it meets. Capacity built into a shortage is accretive if the shortage persists and dilutive if it does not.
- **Product mix.** **NAND grew 382% year-on-year**, with **32GB eMMC in mass production** from 2Q26; **NOR** benefits from HBM4-driven content growth; **Switch 2 ROM** is the stable base. The balance between the volatile and the stable determines how much of the current earnings power persists.
- **Restocking versus run-rate demand.** Whether monthly growth of **+216%** reflects genuine consumption or customers rebuilding inventory after end-of-life notices.

Bottom line: Macronix ended **ten consecutive loss-making quarters** and, within two quarters, went from a **13.2% gross margin to 64.4%** and from **−NT$0.15 to +NT$3.91 per share** — because **Samsung discontinued MLC NAND, Kioxia issued end-of-life notices, and AI servers moving to HBM4 raised NOR content by about 50%**, leaving Macronix serving demand the majors had abandoned. The balance sheet came through intact and the cash is real. But **the advantage was created by competitors' withdrawal**, the company has committed **NT$15.8bn of capital into the conditions that produced it**, and its own record — **NT$4.85 in FY2022, then three years of losses** — is the best available description of what memory does. Judge it on **gross margin and competitor capacity announcements** — a genuine, well-evidenced inflection in the most cyclical business in semiconductors.
